Bound the area with the largest circles

question: In a plane, four circles with radii \(1,\) \(3,\) \(5,\) and \(7\) are tangent to line \(\ell\) at the same point \(A,\) but they may be on either side of \(\ell.\) Region \(S\) consists of all the points that lie inside exactly one of the four circles. What is the maximum possible area of region \(S?\)
solution:
Circles on the same side of \(\ell\) are nested, so only the two largest circles on each side determine the area inside exactly one circle.

To see the nesting, recall that the radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent line. Thus every center lies on the perpendicular to \(\ell\) through \(A\). For two radii \(R>r\) on the same side, the centers are \(R-r\) apart. The smaller disk therefore lies inside the larger disk, touching it at \(A\). Disks on opposite sides have disjoint interiors.

On a side containing at least two circles, a point is inside exactly one circle precisely when it is inside the largest but outside the second-largest. All smaller disks are contained in the second-largest. Thus that side contributes \(\pi(R^2-r^2)\), where \(R\) and \(r\) are its two largest radii. A side with just one circle contributes its whole disk area.

Fix the radius-\(7\) circle on one side. Reflecting an arrangement across \(\ell\) preserves its area, so this loses no possibilities. Each of the other three circles can be on either side, giving the following eight assignments. The entries in the last column use the rule just established.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{Radii on the side with }7 & \text{Radii on the other side} & \text{Area of }S\text{ divided by }\pi\\
\hline
7,5,3,1 & \text{none} & 49-25=24\\
7,5,3 & 1 & 49-25+1=25\\
7,5,1 & 3 & 49-25+9=33\\
7,3,1 & 5 & 49-9+25=65\\
7,5 & 3,1 & 49-25+9-1=32\\
7,3 & 5,1 & 49-9+25-1=64\\
7,1 & 5,3 & 49-1+25-9=64\\
7 & 5,3,1 & 49+25-9=65
\end{array}
\]
Every assignment appears once, according to which subset of \(\{1,3,5\}\) lies opposite the radius-\(7\) circle. The largest area is therefore \(\boxed{65\pi}\), choice \(\textbf{D}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The circles of radii \(7\) and \(5\) control most of the available area, so separate the arrangements according to whether these two circles lie on the same side of \(\ell\).

First, tangency forces all centers onto the perpendicular to \(\ell\) through \(A\). Same-side circles of radii \(R>r\) have center distance \(R-r\), so the smaller disk is contained in the larger. Opposite-side disks have disjoint interiors. Consequently, on a side with several circles, the exactly-one region is the largest disk with the second-largest disk removed.

If radii \(7\) and \(5\) are on the same side, that side contributes
\[
(7^2-5^2)\pi=24\pi.
\]
The other side contains only circles of radii at most \(3\), so it contributes at most \(9\pi\). The total is at most \(33\pi\).

If radii \(7\) and \(5\) are on opposite sides, their disks have combined area
\[
(7^2+5^2)\pi=74\pi.
\]
Every smaller disk is contained in whichever of these two disks is on its side. In particular, every point inside the radius-\(3\) circle lies inside at least two circles, so its entire \(9\pi\) of area is excluded from \(S\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{Area}(S)\le 74\pi-9\pi=65\pi.
\]
This bound is attained by placing radius \(7\) alone on one side and radii \(5,3,1\) on the other. The radius-\(1\) disk is already inside the excluded radius-\(3\) disk, so the resulting area is
\[
49\pi+(25-9)\pi=\boxed{65\pi}.
\]
The answer is \(\textbf{D}\).
